sources.headline: Fires break out at French schools as students protest nationwide
sources.text: Fires have broken out at several schools in France, as students protest by blockading education institutions nationwide over school funding and studying conditions.Blazes were reported at two high schools in Nantes, western France, while another was filmed engulfing the entrance of a school in the northern city of Rouen.Students are protesting about a lack of teachers and staff, overcrowded classrooms and run-down buildings. University students joined the demonstrations on Thursday, citing similar demands.The interior ministry said 1,949 people had been arrested on Thursday, with 305 police officers injured. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu held a crisis meeting on Thursday to discuss the unrest.The government said afterwards that the student-led demonstrations had descended into "urban violence".Both fires in Nantes spread after a bin was set alight. The blaze at the Nelson Mandela high school, in the city centre, then spread to the front of the building, damaging the entrance hall.In the southern city of Marseille, staff at Victor Hugo high school were splashed with petrol as protesters reportedly filled containers.While in the north, a headteacher at Degrugillier high school, in the village of Auchel, was injured in the ear by a wayward firework.The blockades and protests at French lycées - for 15-18 year olds and equivalent to sixth forms in the UK or high schools in the US - began last week before spreading to hundreds of schools across the country.So far, 1,027 lycees have been affected by demonstrations, with blockades at 222 of them, according to the interior ministry.At least 30 universities have also reportedly been blockaded, including campuses in Rennes and Paris.On Thursday, public transport services in Marseille and Strasbourg were halted due vandalism, threats of violence and to hinder protesters from moving around.Seventeen-year-old Raphael took part in protests outside a school in Strasbourg, where barriers were used to obstruct nearby tram tracks. He voiced his frustration at his school's facilities in an interview with news agency AFP, saying some rooms had leaks and that there were not enough toilets."The building is falling apart, the cafeteria is too small. There's zero budget, zero resources, not enough supervisors," Raphael said.While France's next general election is still months away, the protests and how French authorities are responding to them has been heavily politicised.The government and hard-right politicians have blamed the hard left for igniting protests, which are being organised by a union representing lycée students.Bally Bagayoko, the mayor of a Parisian suburb and member of the radical left La France Insoumise (LFI) party defended earlier remarks in which he said violence could be legitimate in some cases - referencing cases in which protesters had allegedly been shot at while not wearing helmets or bulletproof vests.LFI leader and presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon, meanwhile, stressed he was in favour of non-violent protests, while arguing that blaming the left would not solve the issues motivating the demonstrations.Earlier, leader of the hard-right National Rally Marine Le Pen said: "This is no longer about high school student protests. It is about riots organized by professionals and overseen by deputies from La France Insoumise."The presidential candidate called for a new anti-rioting law to be passed.Left-wing mayor of Marseille Benoît Payan condemned the "unacceptable violence" in his city. While young people were "legitimately concerned" about their future and public services, they must express themselves in a calm fashion, he said.Eric Ciotti, the Republicans mayor of Nice, said the parents of those found to have damaged school property should be made to pay for the repairs.

sources.headline: France school protests escalate into ‘urban violence’ as PM calls crisis cabinet meeting
sources.text: A fast-growing protest by high-school students over long hours, teacher shortages and decaying facilities has escalated into “urban violence”, the French government has warned, as it said many schools would switch to online classes to protect teachers and pupils.The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, called a crisis cabinet meeting on Thursday and told ministers to cancel travel plans to deal with the demonstrations, which erupted in the Paris region last week but have snowballed across the country.Lecornu’s office said: “This upsurge in violence makes it virtually impossible to maintain the continuity of public education and is exposing staff and students to danger.” The education minister, Édouard Geffray, is to meet pupil representatives on Friday.About 900 demonstrations, blockades and related incidents were under way outside high schools around the country, police said, with more than 160 shut down as a result. Access was also blocked to about 30 university campuses on Thursday, including in Paris and Marseille.The pupils’ grievances range from overloaded timetables and overcrowded classes to insufficient teachers and unbearable temperatures during heatwaves. Photograph: CLPress/Abaca/ShutterstockNearly 3,000 lycée students – aged between 15 and 18 – have been detained since the start of the protests, including 1,949 on Thursday alone, the interior ministry said. More than 300 police and dozens of firefighters, teachers and pupils have been injured.The pupils’ grievances range from overloaded timetables and overcrowded classes to insufficient teachers and unbearable temperatures during heatwaves earlier this year. Riot police have been deployed to confront the increasingly violent protests.Injuries have mainly been from hurled objects but also from police-fired riot-control projectiles, with the interior ministry announcing an internal police investigation after accusations of excessive force and brutality by officers against three pupils.Rubbish bins have been set on fire outside many schools and more serious arson attempts have been reported inside some buildings. Fire damage in one school in Nantes in the north-west was so extensive that it will stay closed for a month, authorities said.Riot police have been deployed to confront the increasingly violent protests. Photograph: Miguel Medina/AFP/Getty ImagesIn the northern city of Caen, 16-year-old Maelle said she wished those setting bins on fire would protest “with words”. Students were protesting “against this government that doesn’t invest in heating, air conditioning, or teachers’ salaries”, she told AFP.In Strasbourg in the north-east, tram services were temporarily suspended to “restrict the movements of rioters and demonstrators”, the regional prefect said, after protesting students obstructed the tracks with crowd control barriers.“There are 35 of us per classroom,” one 17-year-old Strasbourg student said. “There aren’t enough toilets, and there are water leaks in some rooms. The building is falling apart, the cafeteria is too small. There’s zero budget, zero resources.”Several bin fires were also reported in the southern city of Toulouse; while in Lille, young people wearing black hoodies destroyed a bus stop. In Marseille, there were attempts to light fires inside two schools. In one, a teacher was splashed with petrol.Injuries have mainly been from hurled objects but also from police-fired riot-control projectiles. Photograph: Miguel Medina/AFP/Getty ImagesWhile many teachers and several headteachers have reported being physically threatened and sometimes attacked, some support their pupils. Juliette Estiville, a high-school Spanish teacher in Paris, said that the police response had disgusted her.“I’m actually here just to provide protection, to form a barrier between the police and the students,” she said. “Today went well, it’s going well, but I think that the teachers who come to the blockades are really there to protect our young people.”The government has accused the radical left La France Insoumise (LFI) party of encouraging the protests, with several LFI MPs and mayors, including Bally Bagayoko, the LFI mayor of the Paris suburb of Saint-Denis, cheered at demonstrations.The party’s candidate for the 2027 presidential election, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, insisted on Thursday that LFI backed “non-violent methods of struggle” and added that his “greatest worry is an unbearable level of police violence against these young people”.

sources.headline: School protests spread as fires, blockades deepen unrest in France
sources.text: Police have detained hundreds as students protest overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages and crumbling facilities.French students have set fire to bins and erected blockades outside schools in several cities, protesting overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages and crumbling facilities.Several school principals were injured, harassed or assaulted during blockades at high schools on Thursday, according to reports from regional education authorities, prefectures and union representatives.Recommended Stories list of 2 itemslist 1 of 2Public workers in France strike over pay as student protests turn violentlist 2 of 2What’s behind French student protests that turned violent?end of listPolice have already detained hundreds of protesters at the lycees, which students aged 15 to 18 attend for their final three years of secondary education in France.At Marseille’s Victor Hugo high school, the teachers were inadvertently splashed as a student attempted to throw petrol into a rubbish bin, local authorities said. Earlier, the prosecutor’s office had ⁠said the teachers had been assaulted and “doused in petrol”.At another school in the city, Saint-Exupery high school, hundreds of young people surrounded a firetruck that had arrived to put out a blaze in the morning, police said. The attackers forced the firefighters to flee the vehicle, then set it alight.In Nantes, firefighters extinguished a fire at a high school entrance following what regional education officials called a gathering “marked by violence towards staff”. In Strasbourg, trams were halted to “restrict the movements of rioters and demonstrators”, and students burned barriers on tram tracks, authorities said.“There are 35 of us per classroom. With 35 degrees Celsius [95 degrees Fahrenheit] in summer, it’s unbearable. There aren’t enough toilets, and there are water leaks in some rooms,” Raphael, a 17-year-old who withheld his surname for fear of reprisals, told the AFP news agency outside a protest in Strasbourg.“The building is falling apart, the cafeteria is too small. There’s zero budget, zero resources, not enough supervisors.”His frustration echoes a wave of student anger that has spread across France since last week, as high school pupils protest and grievances snowball into nationwide unrest.Some 340 demonstrations were under way outside high schools by mid-morning on Thursday, with more than 160 schools shut down as a result, police said.University students joined in, blocking access to about 30 campuses, including in Paris and Marseille, according to a student union.Authorities have reported many dozens of injuries – some from thrown objects, others reportedly from police riot-control projectiles.Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said police have opened internal investigations into brutality allegations involving three students.Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu convened a crisis meeting and asked ministers to cancel upcoming official travel so authorities could focus on the demonstrations, his office said.French Education Minister Edouard Geffray said that he would successively meet representative staff unions and parent and student associations on Friday.The unrest has become entangled in the race to succeed President Emmanuel Macron next May. The government has accused the far-left France Unbowed party of encouraging the protests. Presidential candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon said Wednesday that his party “called for nonviolent methods of struggle” and criticised the government’s response as repressive.A student holds a board reading, ‘We want the BAK [high school diploma], not the BAC [anti-criminality units]’ during a protest to demand more resources at school, in Lille, France [Jean-Francois Badias/AP]

sources.headline: France: Hundreds arrested as student protests escalate
sources.text:
Security forces in France on Wednesday detained over 600 people as protests at high schools in parts of the country have intensified.
Authorities said violent clashes and arson attacks have also left dozens of security personnel wounded.
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez condemned what he called an "escalation of violence" outside certain schools.
The violence left 83 police officers and gendarmes wounded on Wednesday, he said, adding that 32 teachers and pupils were also injured. The protests affected 356 schools, the minister noted.
He slammed the "targeting of law enforcement officers, the throwing of projectiles, acts of violence, verbal abuse, attempted arson, and what amounts... to urban violence."The student protest movement began in the Ile-de-France region around the capital, Paris, but has since spread to other regionsImage: Kenzo Tribouillard/AFP
Why are students protesting?
Teenagers at French lycées (equivalent to US high schools) have been blockading their schools since last week.
They are protesting overcrowded classes, heavy workloads, poor-quality learning materials and teacher shortages.
"There are cockroaches and rats everywhere in the school," Fadila, a 17-year-old student, told the Reuters news agency. She said temperatures in classrooms could swing from sweltering to below freezing, depending on the weather.
The movement began in the Ile-de-France region around the capital, Paris, but has since spread to other regions.
The cities worst affected Wednesday include Paris, Bordeaux in the southwest and Lyon in the southeast, and the northern city of Lille, where police again used tear gas in clashes, the AFP news agency reported.What did the government say?
President Emmanuel Macron said the young people's concerns were legitimate but could in no way justify violence and attacks on police officers and teachers, among others.
"High schools are meant to be open and to share knowledge. They are not meant to be blockaded or to have trash ⁠cans set on fire," he told reporters in Madrid.Teenagers at French lycees have been blockading their schools since last weekImage: Raphael Lafargue/ABACA/IMAGO
Both Macron and Nunez accused far-left groups of inciting violence during the protests.
"We observed that, in certain places, ⁠there were ​individuals acting as agitators — people who, moreover, moved from one school to another to stir ​up high school and other students and incite them to commit acts of violence," Nunez said.
Over the past few days, officials and politicians have denounced the left-wing La France Insoumise (France Unbowed or LFI) party and its presidential candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon for rhetoric they said was stoking students' anger.
On Monday, Melenchon had accused the government of implementing a "crackdown" with "obvious racist undertones."
"Hands off our youth!" he wrote on social media, while encouraging LFI activists and officials to support the protests wherever they could.
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu called the accusation of racism "an insult" and accused Melenchon of "racializing a debate about student security and adding to division where a responsible politician should be looking to restore calm."
Edited by: Sean Sinico

sources.headline: Students face riot police as protests over school conditions escalate in France
French protests over school conditions spread as students set fires and put up blockades
sources.text:
By Jean-Philippe Liabot & Andreas Rogal with AFP
Published on
01/10/2026 - 20:15 GMT+2
A protest movement in France's high schools intensified on Thursday, with students setting fire to bins and erecting blockades outside schools in an increasing number of cities.
The students have been protesting overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages and crumbling facilities.
Several school principals have been injured, harassed or assaulted at high schools, according to reports from regional education authorities, prefectures and union representatives.
Police have already detained hundreds of protesters at the lycées, which students aged 15 to 18 attend for their final three years of secondary education in France. There have been multiple reports of high school students being injured.
University students have now also joined the protest movement, and have blocked access to around 30 campuses across the country.
A security source said there had been 900 blockades or related incidents across the country on Thursday, with more than 160 schools shut down in Paris, Marseille and other cities.
In neighbouring Belgium, there were protests and damage at a handful of schools in the eastern city of Liege, police said.
Protesters demand better conditions
At a Paris high school where students barricaded an entrance, one 18-year-old student said protesters want to target “overloaded schedules, the system, the teachers, people who don’t listen to us, the university application process.”
High school students in France often start classes at 8 am and remain at school until late afternoon.
“Older people say, ‘Kids, go to school from 8 am to 6 pm every day.’ But you don’t know what that does mentally,” said another Paris high school student.
Clashes in Lille and Paris
In Lille, the protest led to particularly tense scenes. Bins were tipped over onto the road, projectiles were thrown and street furniture was damaged. Police intervened to disperse the demonstrators, charging into them and firing tear gas.
In Paris and in several communes in Île-de-France, clashes also broke out between young people and police. The movement had already led to several hundred arrests since the start of the week, mostly of minors.
Three investigations have also been opened by the IGPN after injuries sustained during blockades. In Tours, a student injured in the head on Wednesday was taken to hospital. According to the public prosecutor, his injuries were consistent with those of a non-lethal rubber bullet.
University students join the movement
After a first nationwide day of action on Tuesday, university students joined the movement on Thursday. Around 30 campuses were blocked, according to the France's leading students' union. Lower secondary schools were also affected in some regions.
Seconday and high school student organisations are calling above all for greater resources, replacement teachers and better teaching conditions. They say they intend to continue protesting, while the government now tries to contain the violence and keep access to schools open.
Political reactions
The government as well as far-right politician Marine Le Pen have accused the hard-left France Unbowed (LFI) party of encouraging the protests.
But LFI's candidate for the 2027 presidential election, Jean-Luc Melenchon, said on Wednesday that his party "called for non-violent methods of struggle".
